cases.title: Stream chart edits without exposing invalid partial output
cases.prompt:
A downstream export service needs to apply the existing chart edits directly to a borrowed std::io::Write sink, including a trait-object writer, without allocating a second buffer containing the entire resulting XML. Add patch::write_chart_edits(xml: &[u8], data: &ChartData, edits: &[ChartEdit], writer: &mut W) -> Result<(), WritePatchError>, with an appropriate generic writer bound. All existing edit operations and their byte preservation semantics must work. Reuse the current edit planner so validation and output do not drift.

Validation failures must leave the writer completely untouched, even when an invalid or overlapping span would only be discovered after earlier valid edits. Once actual writing starts, an I/O failure may leave a prefix; stop and return it as WritePatchError::Io(std::io::Error). Preserve normal Write behavior for short writes, Interrupted, and WriteZero; do not flush or close the caller's writer. Expose validation failures as WritePatchError::Patch(PatchError). The new error must implement Debug, Display and std::error::Error, with the original typed cause available through Error::source. Keep the underlying I/O error, including its custom payload, rather than rebuilding it from its kind or text. Partial output after an I/O error is not a rollback guarantee; document this distinction.

Existing downstream function signatures, exhaustive enum matches, struct-literal construction, error variants, and byte output must remain compatible. Restrict implementation changes to patch.rs and add integration tests under the crate's tests directory. Existing inline tests, other sources, dependencies, manifests, and toolchain are fixed. Internal refactoring is allowed. Avoid new unsafe code, panic recovery, or bypassed checks. The planner's existing replacement/structural fragments may be allocated, but neither the new path nor a helper may materialize or clone the whole input/output XML just to feed the writer. Write new documentation, tests, and response.json in English. Implement the request and run the required build, tests, Clippy and formatting checks.

cases.title: Transfer chart XML ownership with recovery and allocation reuse
cases.prompt:
A downstream editor already owns the chart XML Vec<u8> and wants to reuse its allocation while applying existing edits. Add patch::apply_chart_edits_owned(xml: Vec<u8>, data: &ChartData, edits: &[ChartEdit]) -> Result<Vec<u8>, OwnedPatchError>. The result must have exactly the existing apply_chart_edits output for every supported edit operation. When the final output length fits the original capacity, preserve the original allocation and capacity, including mixed growing/shrinking replacements and structural insertions/deletions. When it does not fit, growth is allowed. Empty edits must return the original allocation unchanged.

Every validation error must return the untouched original bytes, length, capacity and allocation, so the caller can recover or retry. OwnedPatchError must implement Debug, Display and std::error::Error, provide error(&self) -> &PatchError and into_parts(self) -> (Vec<u8>, PatchError), and expose the underlying typed PatchError through Error::source. Errors must remain valid after the borrowed data and edits go out of scope. Reuse the existing planner and preserve its rejection behavior. Do not clone the full input XML or create a second full output buffer to simulate ownership reuse or recovery. Planned replacement/structural fragments may be owned as they already are. Public scanner data can be malformed; invalid ranges and overlaps must return errors without corrupting the original vector.

Existing downstream function signatures, exhaustive enum matches, struct-literal construction, error variants, and byte output must remain compatible. Restrict implementation changes to patch.rs and add integration tests under the crate's tests directory. Existing inline tests, other sources, dependencies, manifests, and toolchain are fixed. Internal refactoring is allowed. Avoid new unsafe code, panic recovery, or bypassed checks. Write new documentation, tests, and response.json in English. Implement the request and run the required build, tests, Clippy and formatting checks.
